one_liner: Hand-vectorised Mojo Mandelbrot kernel (4 x Float64 lanes, escape mask) that runs 1.6x faster than scalar clang -O3 C.
what_it_does: A standalone benchmark program (benchmarks/mandelbrot/mandelbrot.mojo, 104 lines) from a single-author Mojo research repo, not a library. compute(width, height, max_iter) walks an 800x600 grid over re [-2, 1], im [-1.5, 1.5] and returns the sum of every pixel's escape-iteration count as an Int64; it writes no image or pixel buffer. The program takes --width/--height/--max-iter and prints TIME_SECONDS and CHECKSUM lines that scripts/bench.py gates against the C, Rust, NumPy and Python versions.
how_it_is_fast: Explicit SIMD with per-lane masking: four adjacent pixels go into SIMD[DType.float64, 4] vectors, z is advanced with active.select(new, old) so escaped lanes freeze, and the batch stops when a horizontal reduce of the mask reaches zero or max_iter is hit; a scalar loop handles width % 4. The win comes from running four independent iteration chains at once, where the C loop iterates one pixel at a time through a data-dependent while exit that clang does not vectorise, so it executes one serial dependency chain. On arm64 the 4-wide Float64 vector lowers to two 128-bit NEON registers; Mojo targets the host CPU by default (mojo build docs, search snippet), so on x86-64 it can use one 256-bit register, which fits the larger Linux x86_64 CI gap (2.7x) than arm64 (1.6x on M4 Pro, 1.18x on the CI arm64 runner).
when_to_use: As a worked, MIT-licensed pattern for writing a masked escape-time loop with Mojo's built-in SIMD type instead of intrinsics: the compute function is about 60 lines.
When judging whether Mojo's SIMD ergonomics pay off for per-element-independent Float64 loops with a data-dependent exit, compared with C you have not vectorised by hand.

As a checksum-gated harness template: every variant prints TIME_SECONDS and CHECKSUM, and bench.py refuses to report timings unless all checksums agree, which makes it easy to add a C vector-extension variant and measure the fair comparison.
When you need Float64 on Apple Silicon: the repo's Metal GPU port is 7.9x faster at 800x600 but runs in Float32 and misses the checksum by 1,180.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Mojo generates faster code than C: the C baseline is scalar, and a C version using clang ext_vector_type or NEON/AVX intrinsics with the same 4-lane masking is the fair comparison; the repo has none.
Multi-core or GPU rendering: the kernel is single-threaded on a 14-core machine, and the repo's own GPU port is 7.9x (800x600) to 15.4x (4000x3000) faster in Float32.
Anything not shaped like independent SIMD-friendly arithmetic: in the same repo C beats Mojo on sieve (1.05x), word frequency (1.6x), CSV aggregation (2.3x) and JSON parsing (2.3x).
Production image generation: there is no image output and no callable API, and the repo has 0 stars, one author and no issue tracker activity.

Deeply zoomed or highly chaotic regions: each 4-pixel batch keeps iterating until its slowest lane escapes, so throughput drops when neighbouring pixels have very different escape counts (not measured in the repo).

integration.dependencies: Mojo standard library only (SIMD, std.sys.argv, std.time.perf_counter_ns); the repo builds through pixi with the MAX conda channel
integration.min_toolchain: Mojo 1.0.0 (pixi.lock pins mojo-1.0.0-release and max 26.5.0; pixi.toml allows mojo >=1.0.0,<2)
integration.platforms: osx-arm64, linux-64, linux-aarch64 (pixi.toml); Windows only through WSL2
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded program with no shared state; not documented otherwise

gotchas: Build with --fp-mode contract=off (and clang -ffp-contract=off for C): the default contraction fuses zr*zr - zi*zi + re into FMA and drifts the checksum (Mojo by 10, clang -O3 from 42411634 to 42411589), because escape counts near the set boundary are sensitive to rounding. Both published timings use contraction off, so neither side benefits from FMA.

The record's caveat that the Linux CI has no C row is out of date: experiments/2026-09-04-linux-five-category-crosscheck.md pools 3 CI runs (9 trials each) and shows Mojo 0.0493 s vs C 0.1348 s on x86_64 (2.7x) and 0.0923 s vs 0.1093 s on arm64 (1.18x, ratios derived from page data). The gap tracks vector width and core type, consistent with hand vectorisation rather than code generation.

Mojo builds for the host CPU and its features by default (docs snippet), while clang without -march targets a generic baseline; a Mojo binary built on a newer machine may not run on an older one, and the two sides are not built for the same ISA level.

The kernel is untuned even as SIMD code: it reduces the active mask every iteration and squares the new z for the escape test, then squares it again on the next iteration. A tuned C or Mojo SIMD version could be faster, so 1.6x is neither an upper nor a lower bound on what explicit SIMD gives here.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over the Julia and Fortran userfunc_mandelbrot rows in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks when you want an explicit-SIMD code pattern with an exact checksum gate; pick those rows for a scalar-against-scalar language comparison. The LangArena Mojo Nbody entry is the catalogue's same-algorithm Mojo-vs-C row, but it is a single-run 1.07x that appeared only with a toolchain change.
verified_claims_summary: On an Apple M4 Pro under macOS 26.5.2, the Mojo 1.0.0 4-lane SIMD kernel averaged 0.0554 s over 7 runs (after 2 warm-ups) against 0.0904 s for one-pixel-at-a-time C built with Apple clang 21 -O3 -ffp-contract=off (1.63x) and 0.1114 s for scalar Rust, at 800x600 and 500 iterations with identical checksums (42411634). Pooled Linux CI runs on shared GitHub runners give 2.7x on x86_64 and 1.18x on arm64 (derived from page data).
status_note: Active, MIT-licensed single-author research notebook (124 commits, last 2026-09-25, 0 stars, commits co-authored with Claude); the kernel is small enough to copy, but its 1.6x measures hand SIMD against scalar C, which is why it sits at tier D.
